adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The house had been sold in March, and the closing date gave us six weeks to empty it. My brother drove up from Bristol in a van borrowed from a friend, and we started in the attic because neither of us wanted to begin with the rooms we actually remembered. Boxes of Christmas decorations, a broken fan, a suitcase full of hotel receipts from the 1980s. We worked in silence for the first hour, then fell into the ritual of holding things up to each other and asking whether they mattered. Most of them did not.

On the second day I found a paperback wedged behind the water tank, swollen with damp and missing its cover. It was a novel called The Long Afternoon, and I recognized the author's name from the shelf in the front room. I sat down on the landing and read the first chapter standing up, and then the rest of it sitting down. The book is about a widow in a coastal town who takes in a lodger, a young man who claims to be writing a history of the harbor. Nothing much happens for a hundred pages; she cooks, he walks out to the breakwater, they misunderstand each other politely. Then, in the last third, it turns out that the lodger has invented most of his research, and the widow, who has known this for weeks, has been letting him talk because the sound of someone working in the next room was the thing she missed most. The ending is not forgiving. The final chapter is a list of everything she sells after he leaves, itemized with prices, and the effect is devastating.

I had never heard of the book. My mother must have bought it at a jumble sale and forgotten it. I put it in the van instead of the skip.

By the fourth week we had reached the kitchen, which was the worst of it. Every cupboard held a smaller cupboard's worth of things: jam jars, takeaway menus, a drawer of batteries that had leaked into a single blue crust. We ate fish and chips on the floor because the table had gone to the charity shop. My brother said he was sleeping badly. I said I was too. Neither of us mentioned the photograph of the four of us on the beach, which we found in the same envelope as the warranty for a washing machine that had been scrapped in 2009.

The last thing we took out was the piano, which none of us played and which had been out of tune since I was a child. The removal men wrapped it in blankets and carried it down the stairs sideways, one step at a time, while the neighbor held the door. After they drove off the house was only a set of empty rooms with clean rectangles on the walls. I walked through them once, turned off the lights, and posted the keys through the letterbox of the estate agent on the corner.
